name: The Monsoon Reversal & Meghalaya's Wettest Places
scope: The seasonal wind flip that drowns South Asia, deepened across the wettest inhabited places on Earth. T1: in the hills of Meghalaya in northeast India, the village of Mawsynram catches about 11,800 mm of rain a year -- the wettest inhabited place on Earth (invert the wonder: the huge number is the hook, the PLACE is the answer). T2: neighboring Cherrapunji (Sohra) once collected about 26,470 mm in a single year, 1860-61 -- a genuine 12-month record; answer is Cherrapunji. T2: what soaks them is a WIND REVERSAL -- in summer the land heats faster than the Indian Ocean, air rises over the continent, and the winds swing around to pull wet ocean air onshore (the summer monsoon); answer is the reversing wind / summer monsoon. T3: Meghalaya specifically because the Khasi Hills form a wall that lifts moist air funneling up off the Bay of Bengal (orographic lift); answer is the hills forcing the Bay of Bengal air upward. T4: the Khasi people weave the living aerial roots of the rubber fig (Ficus elastica) into LIVING ROOT BRIDGES across flooded rivers -- bridges that grow stronger for centuries (the double-decker bridge at Nongriat); answer is living root bridges. T4: despite record rain, Cherrapunji suffers dry-season water SHORTAGES because the rain sheets off deforested slopes -- a paradox; answer is dry-season water scarcity. T5: the monsoon 'burst' arrives around June 1 at Kerala and sweeps north; a failed monsoon meant historic famine -- the rains are the heartbeat of a billion farmers; answer is the monsoon onset/burst.
source: Wikipedia: Mawsynram (avg ~11,872 mm; wettest-inhabited claim contested by Colombian sites Lloro/Lopez de Micay); Wikipedia: Cherrapunji (26,470 mm 1860-61 record). Living root bridges of Meghalaya, Khasi Ficus elastica jingkieng jri -- well-established, verify Nongriat double-decker at build. Cross-check Grokipedia at build.
framing_note: Scene-led -- a hillside vanishing behind a wall of rain -- never 'What is the wettest place on Earth?'; put the rainfall number in the stem and make the PLACE the answer. ACCURACY RAIL: 'wettest INHABITED place' is contested (Colombian rivers claim higher averages) -- say 'inhabited' carefully; the 26,470 mm Cherrapunji figure is a real single-year record. Dinner-test payoff = the living root bridges (a cultural creation born of the monsoon). STANCE RAIL (bake into that rung, no ladder-wide mandate): celebrate Khasi root-bridge engineering as sophisticated living architecture, never 'primitive'/'exotic'. LANE: rice paddies get at most a one-rung mention -- rice DISHES belong to the cooking bank. Distractors = other real superlative-rain places (Colombian Choco, Hawaii's Waialeale).

name: El Nino & La Nina -- the Pacific That Shifts the World
scope: The warming and cooling of the tropical Pacific that reshuffles weather across the planet. T1: off the coast of Peru, fishermen long ago named a warm current that arrived around Christmas 'El Nino' -- Spanish for 'the Christ Child'; answer is El Nino (the Christ Child). T2: normally the trade winds pile warm water in the western Pacific and let cold, nutrient-rich water well up off Peru; in an El Nino the winds slacken and the warm water slides BACK east, shutting the upwelling off; answer is the warm water sliding east / upwelling stops. T2: when the cold upwelling dies, Peru's anchovy fishery -- one of the largest on Earth -- collapses; answer is the anchovy-fishery collapse (a place-economy fact, not fish biology). T3: the opposite phase, La Nina ('the little girl'), brings extra-strong trades and an extra-cold eastern Pacific; answer is La Nina. T3: the see-saw of air pressure between Tahiti and Darwin that tracks it is the Southern Oscillation / Walker circulation; answer is the Walker circulation. T4: through 'teleconnections' one warm Pacific patch can dry out Indonesia and Australia (drought, bushfire, failed monsoon) while flooding Peru and the southern US; answer is the worldwide teleconnection/ripple. T4: El Nino years quiet Atlantic hurricanes (extra wind shear) but boost Pacific ones; answer is fewer Atlantic hurricanes. T5: coral and sediment records show ENSO running for thousands of years; a monster El Nino is tied to the catastrophic 1876-78 global famines; answer is the historical famine / the record in corals.
source: Wikipedia: El Nino-Southern Oscillation (Peruvian sailors named warm Christmas current after the Christ Child; Carrillo 1892; anchovy collapses 1972-73/82-83/97-98/2015-16; Walker circulation; teleconnections). Cross-check Grokipedia at build.
framing_note: The name-origin rung respects the religious naming on its own terms -- no smug aside. Dinner-test payoff = the teleconnection (a warm patch of Pacific water lights bushfires in Australia and floods in Peru). ACCURACY RAIL: El Nino = WARM eastern-Pacific phase, La Nina = COOL; do not conflate ENSO with long-term global warming. LANE: the anchoveta is a fish, but the FACT is the fishery/upwelling place-economy, never the fish's anatomy (animal bank). Distractors = other ocean-climate patterns (the monsoon, the Gulf Stream, the North Atlantic Oscillation) -- real but wrong.
history_overlap: The 1876-78 Great Famine (Late Victorian Holocausts) rung could duplicate a history-bank episode on colonial-era famine -- keep geography's answer the El Nino/climate fact and defer the political-history narrative.

name: The Jet Stream -- the River of Wind That Steers the Storms
scope: The fast, narrow ribbon of high wind that flows west-to-east and drives mid-latitude weather. T1: seven miles up over the North Atlantic a band of wind screams along at over 100 mph; a jet from New York to London rides it and lands an hour early, but fights it going the other way; answer is the jet stream. T2: a Japanese meteorologist, Wasaburo Ooishi, discovered it in the 1920s tracking pilot balloons near Mount Fuji -- but published in Esperanto and was ignored for decades; answer is (published in) Esperanto / near Mount Fuji. T2: in WWII Japan floated thousands of paper balloon bombs (fu-go) onto the jet stream to reach North America -- the only WWII attack to kill civilians on the US mainland (six, near Bly, Oregon); answer is the fu-go balloon bombs. T3: the jet forms along the polar front, where cold polar air meets warm subtropical air -- the sharper the temperature contrast, the faster it blows; answer is the polar front / the temperature boundary. T3: it does not run straight -- it snakes in giant Rossby waves, and a deep southward dip drags Arctic air far south (a cold snap); answer is the meander / Rossby-wave dip. T4: when the jet buckles and locks a pattern in place (a blocking high), you get stalled heat domes and week-long floods; answer is a blocking pattern. T5: the polar vortex is a ring of jet-stream wind bottling up Arctic cold; when it weakens, the cold spills south into North America and Europe; answer is the polar vortex.
source: Wikipedia: Jet stream (near tropopause ~30,000 ft, >180 km/h, up to 400 km/h; Ooishi 1920s near Fuji, published in Esperanto and overlooked; Pan Am 1952 Tokyo-Honolulu cut 1/3; WWII fire balloons, six deaths). Fu-go: six killed near Bly, Oregon 1945 -- well-established, verify at build.
framing_note: Scene-led -- a plane pushed early across the Atlantic, a balloon drifting over Oregon -- never 'What is the jet stream?'. Dinner-test payoff = the fu-go balloon bombs (or the Esperanto snub -- both retellable). ACCURACY RAIL: Ooishi published in Esperanto (real reason his 1920s work was ignored); fu-go killed six near Bly, Oregon, May 1945. Place-anchored in Fuji, Oregon, the North Atlantic. Distractors = other wind systems (the trade winds, the Gulf Stream as a WATER current, the Hadley cell).
history_overlap: The WWII fu-go balloon-bomb rung could duplicate a WWII history-bank episode -- keep geography's answer the jet stream / the place, and defer the war narrative to history.

name: The Hadley Cell & the 30-Degree Deserts
scope: The great overturning loop of tropical air that makes rainforests at the equator and deserts at 30 degrees. T1: over the Congo and the Amazon, steamy equatorial air rises and dumps daily rain -- which is why the great rainforests sit in a band right on the equator; answer is the rising equatorial air. T2: that risen air spreads toward the poles high up and comes back DOWN, dry, around 30 degrees latitude -- and that sinking air bakes the Sahara, Arabia, the Kalahari, and Australia's Outback into a belt of deserts; answer is the sinking/descending dry air. T2: the whole loop is the Hadley cell, worked out by George Hadley in 1735 to explain the trade winds; answer is the Hadley cell. T3: sailors called the calm-wind zone under the sinking air the 'horse latitudes' -- legend says becalmed ships threw horses overboard to save water; answer is the horse latitudes (label as legend). T3: where the trade winds of both hemispheres converge and lift, the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) marches north and south with the seasons, dragging the monsoon rains with it; answer is the ITCZ. T4: the descending branch parks semi-permanent high-pressure zones over the oceans -- the Azores High, the Pacific High -- that steer summer storms; answer is the subtropical highs. T5: the Hadley cell is WIDENING as the planet warms, pushing its dry edge poleward and threatening to dry the Mediterranean and California; answer is the expanding/widening dry belt.
source: Wikipedia: Hadley cell (air rises at ITCZ, descends ~30 deg producing subtropical deserts incl. Sahara/Arabian; George Hadley 1735 explained trade winds; clear skies + evaporation surplus in the descending branch). Horse-latitudes etymology = disputed legend. Cross-check Grokipedia at build.
framing_note: INVERT THE WONDER: the deserts-line-up-at-30-degrees pattern is the hook, the sinking Hadley air the answer. Teach 'Hadley cell' and 'ITCZ' before testing them. Dinner-test payoff = the horse latitudes (LABEL the horse-overboard story as legend, not fact -- an accuracy rail). ACCURACY RAIL: not every desert is a Hadley desert -- the Atacama and Gobi are rain-shadow/current deserts (own ladders); keep this ladder's answers the SUBTROPICAL-belt deserts under the descending branch. Distractors = rain-shadow or coastal deserts (real, but formed by a different cause).

name: The Trade Winds & the Doldrums -- the Highways of Sail
scope: The steady tropical winds that carried the Age of Discovery, and the dead-calm belt between them. T1: for five centuries, sailing ships crossing the Atlantic from Europe to the Americas rode a reliable wind blowing steadily from the northeast -- the trade winds; answer is the trade winds. T2: 'trade' here first meant a steady 'track' or course, not commerce -- but the winds became so vital to merchant fleets that the money-meaning stuck; answer is 'a steady track/course' (etymology twist, label as such). T2: Columbus rode the trades WEST from the Canary Islands, then looped home on the higher-latitude westerlies -- the great clockwise wheel of Atlantic wind; answer is the westerlies (the road home). T3: right at the equator the two hemispheres' trade winds collide and cancel into a windless belt -- the doldrums, where sailing ships could sit becalmed for weeks; answer is the doldrums / ITCZ. T3: for 250 years Spanish galleons rode the trades and the Kuroshio from Manila to Acapulco -- the longest sustained trade route in history; answer is the Manila galleon route. T4: the Portuguese 'volta do mar' -- swinging far out toward Brazil to catch the westerlies home from Africa -- was the trick that unlocked ocean navigation; answer is the volta do mar. T5: the trades blow east-to-west because the Coriolis effect bends the equator-bound air; without Earth's spin they would blow straight toward the equator; answer is the Coriolis bend.
source: Wikipedia: Trade winds (etymology 'track' -> later 'commerce'; NE/SE toward equator; doldrums/ITCZ; Portuguese volta do mar, cross to Brazil then east ~30S; enabled colonization of the Americas). Manila galleon route -- well-established, verify at build.
framing_note: STANCE (vision_mandated): CELEBRATE the Age of Discovery and its seamanship honestly, and be honest BOTH WAYS about what the routes carried -- immense wealth and exchange AND colonization and slaving -- plainly, without warping the wind facts. Dinner-test payoff = the doldrums (becalmed for weeks) or the volta do mar counterintuitive detour. ACCURACY RAIL: the 'track not commerce' etymology is the real older meaning -- present it as an etymology twist. LANE: no spice/cargo-as-food ladder (cooking bank). Distractors = other named wind systems (westerlies, monsoon, roaring forties).
history_overlap: The Columbus-westward and Manila-galleon rungs may duplicate Age-of-Discovery voyages in the history bank -- keep geography's answer the WIND / route, not the voyage's political narrative.

name: The Coriolis Effect -- Why the Storms Spin
scope: How Earth's rotation bends every moving wind and sets the storms turning. T1: a hurricane in the Caribbean spins counterclockwise, but a cyclone off Australia spins clockwise -- a perfect mirror image; what flips them is Earth's own rotation; answer is Earth's rotation (the Coriolis effect). T2: named for Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis (1835), the effect nudges anything moving over the spinning globe -- to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, to the left in the Southern; answer is the Coriolis effect / deflection to the right (north). T2: it is why tropical storms almost never form within about 5 degrees of the equator -- there is too little spin there to get them turning; answer is (too little Coriolis) at the equator. T3: long-range gunners had to correct for it -- WWI's Paris Gun, firing 75 miles, drifted noticeably from the Coriolis bend; answer is the Coriolis drift on the shells. T3: the 'which way does the bathtub or toilet drain' story is a MYTH -- a basin is far too small for Coriolis to matter; drain shape and swirl decide it; answer is a myth (label). T4: winds do not flow straight from high to low pressure -- Coriolis bends them until they circle the pressure center (the geostrophic wind); answer is they spiral around the pressure center.
source: Wikipedia: Coriolis force (deflection right in N. Hemisphere / left in S.; storms counterclockwise N / clockwise S; cyclones rarely form within 5 deg of equator; bathtub/toilet drain is a debunked myth; Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis 1835). Paris Gun Coriolis correction -- well-established, verify at build.
framing_note: Teach the effect through scenes -- a storm seen from space, a becalmed equator -- never a bare definition. Dinner-test payoff = the toilet/bathtub-drain MYTH, which doubles as an accuracy rail: debunk it explicitly. ACCURACY RAIL: Coriolis is negligible at household scale; real at storm/artillery scale. Distractors = other real forces or drivers (gravity, magnetism, the jet stream, air pressure) -- keep all four live so the player must KNOW the answer.

name: Rain-Shadow Deserts -- the Dry Side of the Mountains
scope: How a mountain wall wrings the rain out of the air and casts a desert behind it. T1: cross the Andes from the wet Chilean coast and the far side is bone-dry -- Argentine Patagonia is a cold desert sitting in the mountains' 'rain shadow'; answer is the rain shadow (or Patagonia). T2: the mechanism: moist ocean wind climbs the windward slope, cools, and dumps its rain there -- so it clears the crest already wrung dry; answer is the moisture squeezed out on the windward side. T2: behind the Himalaya and the Tibetan Plateau -- the world's highest wall -- lies the Gobi, cut off from the monsoon; answer is the Gobi (the Himalayan rain shadow). T3: in North America the Sierra Nevada casts the shadow that makes the Great Basin and Death Valley, the driest and lowest place on the continent; answer is Death Valley / the Great Basin. T3: on Kauai the windward flank of Mount Waialeale is among the wettest spots on Earth (~11,000 mm) while the leeward Kona-style coast stays sunny-dry -- a rain shadow only miles wide; answer is Mount Waialeale's dry lee. T4: New Zealand's Southern Alps: the West Coast drinks six to seven meters of rain while Central Otago just over the crest is the nation's driest land; answer is the Southern Alps rain shadow / Central Otago. T5: the Judaean Desert lies in the rain shadow of the Judaean hills only miles from the green Mediterranean coast -- a desert beside the sea; answer is the Judaean Desert.
source: Wikipedia: Rain shadow (windward ascent/precipitation, leeward descent/foehn; Atacama & E. Patagonia rain-shadowed by Andes; Gobi/Taklamakan behind Himalayas; Death Valley & Great Basin behind Sierra Nevada/Cascades). Mount Waialeale ~11,500 mm and NZ Southern Alps contrast -- well-established, verify figures at build.
framing_note: Teach 'rain shadow' and 'windward/leeward' before testing them; scene-led -- climb the wet green slope, cross the crest, drop into the dry lee. Dinner-test payoff = Death Valley, or the miles-wide Hawaiian shadow (wettest and driest almost touching). ACCURACY RAIL: the Sahara and Arabia are HADLEY deserts, not rain-shadow -- do not miscredit them; the Atacama gets only ONE passing mention here (its full multi-cause story is a separate ladder). Distractors = deserts formed by a DIFFERENT cause (Sahara=Hadley, Namib=cold current).

name: The Atacama -- the Driest Place on Earth
scope: A hyper-arid Chilean desert made bone-dry by three forces at once, yet full of wonders. T1: in northern Chile's Atacama, some weather stations have NEVER recorded a single drop of rain; answer is the Atacama (the never-rains desert). T2: it is dry for three reasons stacked together -- the Andes block Atlantic moisture (rain shadow), the cold Humboldt Current chills the coast so little water evaporates, and it sits under the sinking Hadley air; the reason people forget is the cold ocean current; answer is the cold Humboldt Current. T3: there is almost no rain but there IS fog -- the camanchaca rolls in off the cold sea, and coastal 'fog oases' (lomas) catch it; people string fog nets to harvest drinking water; answer is the camanchaca fog / fog-catching nets. T3: its soil is so Mars-like and lifeless that NASA tests Mars rovers and life-detection instruments there; answer is (a stand-in for) Mars. T4: once every few years a freak rain triggers the 'desierto florido' -- the desert erupts in a carpet of flowers from long-dormant seeds; answer is the flowering desert (desierto florido). T4: the skies are so clear and dry that some of the world's biggest telescopes -- ALMA and the VLT at Paranal -- are built there; answer is the great observatories / ALMA. T5: preserved by that aridity, the Chinchorro mummies of the Atacama coast are the oldest deliberately made mummies on Earth -- older than Egypt's; answer is the Chinchorro mummies.
source: Wikipedia: Atacama Desert (two-sided rain shadow Andes + Coast Range; cold north-flowing Humboldt Current; South Pacific anticyclone/Hadley subsidence; stations never recorded rain; possibly no significant rain 1570-1971; camanchaca fog supports lichens/cacti; desierto florido Sep-Nov; ALMA/ESO Paranal & La Silla). Chinchorro mummies oldest deliberate mummification -- well-established, verify at build.
framing_note: INVERT THE WONDER throughout -- the 'never rained on record' fact is the hook, the PLACE (and its causes) the answer. The three-causes rung teaches that a great desert can have STACKED drivers (Hadley + rain shadow + cold current) -- but keep it ONE coherent answer (the cold current is the missed piece), not a theory-stack. Dinner-test payoff = the camanchaca fog-nets, or the flowering desert. LANE: the flowering-desert PLANTS and any fog-drinking creature are botany/animal -- keep the answer the PLACE-fact (the bloom, the fog oasis), never species anatomy. Chinchorro rung: respect on its own terms. Distractors = other superlative deserts (Sahara largest, Death Valley hottest, Antarctica coldest/polar).
history_overlap: The Chinchorro-mummies rung could touch a history/archaeology episode -- keep geography's answer the place-fact (aridity preserved the world's oldest mummies) and defer the culture-history detail.

name: Foehn & Chinook -- the Warm Wind Off the Mountains
scope: The dry downslope wind that pours off a mountain's lee side and warms as it falls. T1: in Alberta a warm winter wind spills off the Rockies and can melt a foot of snow in hours -- locals call it the chinook, the 'snow-eater'; answer is the chinook (snow-eater). T2: in Spearfish, South Dakota a chinook once shot the temperature from -4F to 45F in TWO MINUTES -- the fastest temperature change ever recorded; answer is Spearfish (the two-minute jump). T2: why it warms -- air wrung dry going up the peak descends the far side and COMPRESSES, heating as it sinks (the foehn effect); answer is the descending air compresses and warms. T3: in the Alps the original 'foehn' melts the snow and (in folklore) frays people's nerves -- old Alpine courts once treated a foehn day as a mitigating factor; answer is the foehn (Alps), mood-effect labeled folklore. T3: in Southern California the Santa Ana winds are the same beast, and they fan wildfires downslope toward Los Angeles; answer is the Santa Ana winds. T4: Argentina's Zonda drops off the Andes onto Mendoza -- same wind, another name; answer is the Zonda. T4: foehn winds sweeping over Antarctica's ice shelves can melt the surface and help crack them apart; answer is (foehn over) Antarctic ice shelves.
source: Wikipedia: Foehn wind (dry warm downslope lee wind; adiabatic warming; chinook 'snow-eater' Rockies/Alberta; Santa Ana CA; zonda Argentina; can raise temps ~14C in hours). Spearfish SD -4F to 45F in 2 min, Jan 22 1943 = world record -- well-established, verify at build.
framing_note: Scene-led -- snow vanishing off an Alberta field in an afternoon. Dinner-test payoff = the Spearfish two-minute record (an accuracy rail: -4F to 45F, Jan 22 1943). ACCURACY RAIL: the mood/health effects of the foehn are FOLKLORE -- label them so, do not state as fact. Ties to the rain-shadow ladder (same compression-warming physics) but anchor each to a DIFFERENT named place. Distractors = COLD downslope/regional winds that are the opposite (mistral, bora) -- adjacent-but-wrong.

name: The Named Winds -- Mistral, Sirocco, Harmattan, Khamsin
scope: The famous regional winds that rule their coasts, each anchored to a named place. T1: in Provence a cold, dry wind roars down the Rhone valley to the Mediterranean so hard it bends the cypress trees and scrubs the sky brilliant blue -- the mistral; answer is the mistral. T2: the mistral shaped Provencal life -- farmhouses built with blank north walls and rows of cypress windbreaks, and Van Gogh painted lashed to his easel at Arles; answer is (blank north walls / cypress windbreaks). T2: from the south comes its opposite, the sirocco -- a hot wind off the Sahara that carries red dust across the sea and drops 'blood rain' on southern Europe and the Alps; answer is the sirocco (blood rain). T3: in West Africa the harmattan drives dry Saharan dust down to the Gulf of Guinea in a haze that grounds flights -- yet it is so refreshingly dry that locals call it 'the Doctor'; answer is the harmattan (the Doctor). T3: that same Saharan dust, much of it from a single spot -- Chad's Bodele Depression -- blows clear across the Atlantic and FERTILIZES the Amazon rainforest with phosphorus; answer is it fertilizes the Amazon. T4: in Egypt the khamsin ('fifty') is a scorching spring wind named for the roughly fifty days it can recur, burying roads and darkening Cairo's sky; answer is the khamsin. T4: the icy bora off Trieste and the summer meltemi of the Aegean round out the family -- each a named local wind that governs a shoreline; answer is the bora / meltemi.
source: Wikipedia: Sirocco (Saharan hot wind, red 'blood rain' in S. Italy, up to ~100 km/h); Harmattan (dry dusty NE trade Nov-Mar, 'the Doctor', harmattan haze, RH <15%). Mistral (cold dry NW down Rhone, Provencal architecture) and khamsin (~50-day hot Egyptian wind); Saharan dust from Bodele Depression fertilizing Amazon with phosphorus -- all well-established, verify at build.
framing_note: Each rung anchors to a NAMED place and its signature wind; distractors = OTHER named winds (adjacent-but-wrong, all real). The mistral-architecture / Van Gogh rung is a genuine cultural creation shaped by the wind. Dinner-test payoff = Saharan dust crossing the ocean to feed the Amazon (ACCURACY RAIL: verify the Bodele Depression as the dominant source and the phosphorus-fertilization link at build). LANE: no wine-of-Provence or food ladder (cooking bank). Keep hot vs cold winds correctly sorted -- an accuracy rail.

name: Hurricane, Typhoon, Cyclone -- One Storm, Three Names
scope: The single most powerful storm on Earth, wearing a different name in every ocean. T1: the exact same spinning storm is a 'hurricane' over the Caribbean, a 'typhoon' over the Philippines, and a 'cyclone' over India -- three names, one beast; answer is they are the same storm (named by region). T2: at its heart is the eye -- a calm, often sunny circle of still air -- ringed by the eyewall where the deadliest winds howl; answer is the eye. T2: the biggest killer is usually not the wind but the storm surge, a wall of seawater the storm shoves ashore; answer is the storm surge. T3: the deadliest on record was the 1970 Bhola cyclone in the Bay of Bengal -- up to half a million dead in what is now Bangladesh, because the funnel-shaped bay magnifies the surge; answer is the Bay of Bengal / Bhola. T3: they only spin up over ocean warmer than about 26.5C and never right on the equator (no Coriolis spin to start them turning); answer is warm water, not on the equator. T4: the Saffir-Simpson scale rates them 1 to 5 by wind; a Category 5 like Typhoon Haiyan (2013, Philippines) or the 1935 Labor Day hurricane (Florida Keys) erases everything in its path; answer is Category 5. T4: Typhoon Tip (1979, NW Pacific) was the largest ever measured -- about 2,220 km across, as wide as the western United States; answer is Typhoon Tip. T5: Hurricane Catarina (2004) was the first hurricane ever recorded in the South Atlantic, a basin where they 'should not' form; answer is the South Atlantic / Catarina.
source: Wikipedia: Tropical cyclone (hurricane=Atlantic/NE Pacific, typhoon=NW Pacific, cyclone=Indian Ocean/S Pacific; eye 30-65 km calm, eyewall strongest; storm surge deadliest; needs Coriolis, rarely forms within 5 deg of equator). Bhola cyclone 1970 (deadliest, ~300k-500k), Typhoon Tip 1979 (~2,220 km), Hurricane Catarina 2004 (first S. Atlantic) -- well-established, verify figures at build.
framing_note: The three-names fact is the spine; scene-led -- a satellite eye, a drowned coast -- never 'What is a hurricane?'. Dinner-test payoff = Typhoon Tip's continent-spanning size, or the one-storm-three-names reveal itself. ACCURACY RAILS: the Bhola death toll is an ESTIMATE/range (label it); ~26.5C and the ~5-degree-Coriolis limit are real thresholds; distinguish the Saffir-Simpson wind scale from actual damage. Distractors = other storm types (tornado, nor'easter, derecho) and other named storms -- keep all four live.
history_overlap: The 1970 Bhola cyclone's role in triggering Bangladesh's independence could duplicate a history-bank episode -- keep geography's answer the storm / the Bay of Bengal and defer the political aftermath to history.

name: The Gulf Stream -- the Ocean River That Warms Europe
scope: The warm current that carries Caribbean heat to Europe and drives a planet-spanning conveyor. T1: London sits as far north as icy Labrador in Canada, yet has mild, palm-friendly winters -- because a warm ocean river, the Gulf Stream, ferries tropical heat across the Atlantic; answer is the Gulf Stream. T2: its warmth lets western Scotland and Ireland grow palm trees and keeps Norway's Arctic ports ice-free all winter; answer is (ice-free) Norway / palms in Scotland. T2: Benjamin Franklin, as colonial postmaster, first charted it in 1769 to explain why westbound mail ships were slower -- the first map of the current; answer is Benjamin Franklin's 1769 chart. T3: it moves roughly 30 million cubic meters of water a second past Florida -- more than all the world's rivers combined; answer is (more than) all the rivers combined. T3: it is one arm of a global conveyor -- the thermohaline circulation -- where cold, salty water sinks near Greenland and pulls the warm surface water north; answer is the global conveyor / sinking near Greenland. T4: scientists watch that conveyor (the AMOC) for a SLOWDOWN -- a big weakening could chill northwest Europe even as the planet as a whole warms; answer is it could cool Europe. T4: the cold, opposite-flowing currents do the reverse -- the Humboldt off Peru and the Benguela off Namibia chill their coasts and build coastal deserts; answer is the Humboldt / Benguela (cold currents). T5: where the warm Gulf Stream collides with the cold Labrador Current off Newfoundland, fog and fish teem -- the Grand Banks, once the richest fishery on Earth; answer is the Grand Banks.
source: Wikipedia: Gulf Stream (warms NW/N Europe vs same-latitude Canada; ice-free Norwegian coast, Tromso; Franklin/Folger 1769 chart; ~30 Sv at Florida rising to ~150 Sv; thermohaline sinking to North Atlantic Deep Water; IPCC AR6 slowdown not shutdown). Grand Banks (Gulf Stream x Labrador Current) -- well-established, verify at build.
framing_note: INVERT THE WONDER: 'London is as far north as Labrador' is the hook, the warm current the answer. Franklin rung is anchored to a real 1769 chart -- keep it a light touch, not a biography. Dinner-test payoff = the counterintuitive twist that a WARMING planet could FREEZE Europe if the conveyor stalls. ACCURACY RAIL: IPCC finds AMOC likely to slow, not shut down this century -- state it as slowdown/risk, not a coming ice age. Distractors = other real currents (Kuroshio, California Current, Humboldt) -- adjacent-but-wrong.
history_overlap: Benjamin Franklin's 1769 Gulf Stream chart is a light history/science touch -- keep geography's answer the current / the chart, not a Franklin biography.

name: Antarctica -- the Windiest, Coldest Place on Earth
scope: The frozen continent that holds the planet's records for wind and cold, driven by air pouring off the ice. T1: at Commonwealth Bay in Antarctica the wind blows near gale force almost every day and has gusted past 300 km/h -- the windiest place at sea level on Earth; answer is Commonwealth Bay (the katabatic coast). T2: these are katabatic winds -- freezing, dense air sliding downhill off the high ice sheet under gravity, funneling and accelerating as it races to the coast; answer is katabatic (downhill) winds. T2: Douglas Mawson's 1911-14 team lived in that gale and he titled his account 'The Home of the Blizzard'; answer is 'The Home of the Blizzard'. T3: high on the inland plateau, Vostok Station recorded -89.2C (-128.6F) in 1983 -- the coldest air temperature ever measured on Earth; answer is Vostok Station. T3: two miles beneath Vostok lies a hidden liquid lake -- Lake Vostok -- sealed under the ice for millions of years; answer is Lake Vostok. T4: the wind-scoured McMurdo Dry Valleys may not have seen rain in two million years -- the closest thing on Earth to the surface of Mars; answer is the Dry Valleys. T4: Antarctica's ice holds around 90 percent of the planet's ice and most of its fresh water; answer is (most of Earth's) ice / fresh water.
source: Wikipedia: Cape Denison / Commonwealth Bay (Mawson called it the windiest place on Earth; fierce katabatic winds; 'Home of the Blizzard'). Vostok Station -89.2C on 21 Jul 1983 (coldest surface air record); Lake Vostok subglacial lake; McMurdo Dry Valleys -- well-established, verify at build.
framing_note: INVERT THE WONDER: the 300 km/h gusts are the hook, the PLACE the answer. Teach 'katabatic'. Dinner-test payoff = the Vostok cold record. ACCURACY RAIL: -89.2C (1983) is the coldest AIR temperature at a weather station -- satellites later found colder ICE-SURFACE spots on the plateau; say 'air temperature' so both stay true. LANE: penguins and seals are the animal bank -- keep every answer the PLACE (the wind, the cold, the dry valleys, the ice), never a creature's biology. Distractors = other extreme places (Death Valley hottest, Atacama driest non-polar, Commonwealth Bay windiest).
history_overlap: Mawson's 1911-14 Australasian Antarctic Expedition is a light exploration-history touch -- keep geography's answer the place / the wind and defer the expedition narrative to history.

name: Tornado Alley & the Supercell
scope: The stretch of North America that breeds more tornadoes than anywhere on Earth, and why. T1: the central US Great Plains -- Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, Nebraska -- see more tornadoes than any place on the planet; the belt is nicknamed 'Tornado Alley'; answer is Tornado Alley. T2: the recipe is a collision: cold, dry air spilling east off the Rockies rides OVER warm, wet air streaming up from the Gulf of Mexico, and the unstable layers erupt upward into rotating supercell thunderstorms; answer is the clash of Rockies-dry over Gulf-moist air. T2: the sharp boundary where dry desert air meets Gulf moisture -- the 'dryline,' often over the Texas Panhandle -- is where the storms fire; answer is the dryline. T3: the widest tornado ever measured struck El Reno, Oklahoma in 2013 -- about 2.6 miles (4.2 km) across; answer is El Reno. T3: Ted Fujita built the scale (F, now EF) that rates tornado damage from EF0 to EF5 -- only an EF5 peels pavement and levels a brick house; answer is the Fujita scale. T4: 'Dixie Alley' across the Deep South is often deadlier -- its tornadoes strike at night, hidden in rain and trees; answer is Dixie Alley.
source: Well-established meteorology: Tornado Alley (Great Plains, US leads world in tornado count); supercell ingredients (Rocky Mtn dry air over Gulf moisture, the dryline); El Reno OK 31 May 2013 widest on record ~4.2 km; Ted Fujita / (Enhanced) Fujita scale; Dixie Alley nocturnal/rain-wrapped risk. Verify all figures against Wikipedia + Grokipedia at build.
framing_note: Scene-led -- a green-black sky and a lowering wall cloud -- never 'What is a tornado?'. Dinner-test payoff = the El Reno widest-tornado record (ACCURACY RAIL: ~2.6 mi / 4.2 km wide, 31 May 2013 -- widest by radar; note it was rated EF3, not the strongest). ANIMAL/LANE: none. Distractors = other severe-weather features/places (derecho, haboob, hurricane, Dixie Alley) -- adjacent-but-wrong. Teach 'supercell' and 'dryline' before leaning on them.
